Since cervical cancer can have a subtle and slow onset, it is important to remember that pap smears are an effective screening method that has drastically decreased the rates of cervical cancer in the United States. Recommendations for which women should receive pap smears and how often has changed over recent years due to efforts to provide adequate screening without over-testing and subjection to unnecessary invasive procedures. Current guidelines recommend beginning pap smears at age 21 and performing them every 3-5 years depending on age, history, and type of test (cytology versus cytology with HPV co-testing). With a history of negative pap smears, testing can be stopped at age 65. Testing can also cease following a hysterectomy for benign disease such as uterine fibroids. Various algorithms are provided by the America Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Patholgy (ASCCP) for follow-up and management based on the degree of cellular changes seen, presence of HPV infection, and other factors.

It is also important to consider that new methods of HPV vaccines are a new method of primary prevention that have shown promising preliminary data on decreasing changes related to early cervical dysplasia. This case of Ms. Pauls reminds you to consider HPV vaccination in all of your younger patients for primary prevention of cervical dysplasia and cancer by preventing infection with HPV. Gardasil and Cervarix are the two current HPV vaccines on the market. Gardasil was initially approved in the United Sates in 2006 and in most states by 2008. Due to the latency period of 10-20 years between HPV exposure and cervical cancer development, it is hard to definitively show that HPV vaccination reduces risk of cervical cancer currently (2015). However, studies in the United States have shown a decrease in high-grade cervical dysplasia in some states with increased vaccination rate. The vaccine contains recombinant HPV capsid proteins that form virus-like particles (VLPs), which lead to an immune response of high levels of neutralizing antibody. The original Gardasil acts against HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. The newer nine-valent Gardasil-based vaccine also protects against other risk subtypes of 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. Gardasil is administered in a series of three shots over a six month period recommended for girls and boys age 11-12 as to precede sexarche and has been tested in ages 9-26. Cervarix is a competitor vaccine approved in 2009 that acts against subtypes 16 and 18. It is recommended for girls age 11-12. Vaccines are not expected to cause regression of established lesions which speaks to the importance of vaccination prior to sexarche.
SBP: It is important to consider social issues and barriers to patient follow-up, especially in patients who have a previously track record of noncompliance or physician avoidance. It is also important to provide constant reassurance on the side effects of chemotherapy and radiation and ensure that she is connected to community resources to provide guidance for supports including wigs for hair loss. Another important consideration is making sure that Ms. Pauls has a support system at home and has friends and family that will be able to provide both emotional and direct support. It is also common for patients to experience depression, so it is import for her to be connected with her primary care physician or a psychiatrist during this process. Her primary care physician will be important in this collaboration as she will need to be assessed for chronic medical conditions such as hypertension and diabetes since she has not seen a provider in some time.
